analysis.one_liner: Bars employers from cutting workers' health coverage during a strike or lockout.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat without action in the House Education and Workforce Committee since its referral in May 2025, with 55 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change federal labor law so that an employer cannot terminate or change an employee's health insurance while the employer is locking workers out or while workers are on a lawful strike [S2]. Today, an employer can cut off health coverage during a labor dispute, which can force striking workers to give in quickly. The bill would make that an unfair labor practice and would let the National Labor Relations Board impose civil penalties of up to $75,000 per violation during a lockout and $50,000 during a strike, with penalties doubled for repeat offenders, and would allow penalties against individual company directors and officers [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Striking and locked-out workers and their families keep their employer-provided health insurance during labor disputes, instead of losing coverage precisely when they can least afford it [S2]. Unions gain leverage in collective bargaining because employers can no longer use health coverage as pressure [S2].

how_it_helps.text: It makes it an unfair labor practice for an employer to terminate or alter an employee's group health plan coverage during a lockout or a lawful strike.
It adds civil penalties of up to $75,000 per violation for cutting coverage during a lockout and $50,000 during a strike, doubled for repeat offenders whose actions seriously harm employees.
It lets the National Labor Relations Board hold individual directors and officers personally liable when they direct, commit, or fail to prevent the violation.

analysis.who_pays: Employers involved in strikes or lockouts, who would have to maintain health coverage for striking or locked-out workers and face civil penalties of up to $75,000 (or $150,000 for repeat offenders) per violation, plus possible personal liability for directors and officers [S2].

drawbacks.text: Employers facing strikes or lockouts would have to keep paying health plan coverage for striking or locked-out employees, raising the cost of a labor dispute for the company.

The bill attaches civil penalties of up to $75,000 per violation (doubled to $150,000 for repeat offenders causing serious harm) and allows the labor board to hold individual directors and officers personally liable, which employers view as excessive enforcement power.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to workers is direct and significant: health coverage is often the breaking point in a strike, and employers can currently cut it off to force concessions; this bill would remove that weapon [S2]. The costs are real but limited: employers would bear the risk of continued premium payments during disputes and face civil penalties up to $150,000 per violation, with personal liability possible for executives [S2]. Critics would argue this raises the cost of managing labor disputes and limits employer leverage at the bargaining table. On balance the bill is narrowly targeted at one coercive tactic rather than broadly restructuring labor law.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee and has sat there with no action since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 21, 2025, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — has been taken since the referral.
All 55 cosponsors are House Democrats; no Republicans signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers retain the ability to cut health coverage during strikes and lockouts, and labor unions lose a potential bargaining protection.

for.name: Rep. Chris Deluzio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sponsored it.

against.name: House Education and Workforce Committee leadership
against.role: House committee with jurisdiction over labor law
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after its referral — no hearing, markup, or floor vote has occurred.

sides.party_line_note: All 55 cosponsors are House Democrats and the bill has no Republican cosponsors; it sits in a committee chaired by the Republican majority [S3][S1].

industries.note: Companies facing strikes or lockouts would lose the ability to pressure workers by cutting off their health coverage, and would face civil penalties up to $150,000 per violation, including possible personal liability for executives.
Unions gain leverage in bargaining because members no longer risk losing family health coverage for exercising the right to strike or being locked out.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors, no committee action since May 2025, and a Republican majority controlling the House floor, the bill is unlikely to receive a hearing or vote in this Congress; similar bills have repeatedly died in committee.
